scenes.visual: Title card 'Relatedness Lives at the Nodes' fades in over a faint outline of the five-tip tree. THE WORLD, kept for both films (16:9, warm cream background). One horizontal tree, root on the left, tips on the right, five tips top to bottom: lamprey, shark, trout, frog, human, each with a simple flat cartoon icon (no photographs). Internal nodes are small circles labelled R (root), J, B, T. COLOUR MAP, same in every scene of both films: branches dark charcoal; node B GOLD (the trout-human most recent common ancestor); node J GREY-BLUE; nodes R and T plain charcoal; a derived state TEAL; an ancestral state light GREY; trace lines from tips back to nodes are the colour of the node they reach. A thin time arrow under the tree points right, labelled 'older' at the left and 'today' at the right. Tree drawings are schematic, not to time scale.

scenes.tts: Is a trout more closely related to a shark, or to you? The two fish look alike. A tree gives a different answer.
scenes.visual: Three cartoon cards side by side: shark, trout, human. The shark and trout cards slide together and a faint 'looks alike' bracket joins them. A question mark appears over the human card.
scenes.narration: Is a trout more closely related to a shark, or to you? The two fish look alike. A tree gives a different answer.

scenes.tts: A phylogenetic tree is a hypothesis about ancestry. The living species sit at the tips. Here are five: lamprey, shark, trout, frog and human. Nobody watched these lineages split. The tree is estimated from characters, usually DNA or protein sequences.
scenes.visual: The cards shrink and fly to the right edge, becoming the five tip icons in order lamprey, shark, trout, frog, human. Branches grow leftward from them and join. A small strip of letters (schematic sequence, 'ACGT...') scrolls under the tree, labelled 'estimated from sequences'.
scenes.narration: A phylogenetic tree is a hypothesis about ancestry. The living species sit at the tips. Here are five: lamprey, shark, trout, frog and human. Nobody watched these lineages split. The tree is estimated from characters, usually DNA or protein sequences.

scenes.tts: Each point where a branch splits is an internal node. It stands for an inferred ancestor of every lineage descending from it. The root, on the left, is the ancestor of everything on the tree.
scenes.visual: The four internal node circles pop in one by one, R, J, B, T, each with a dashed 'inferred ancestor' tag. When J lights, every branch to its right briefly brightens to show 'descends from J'. R pulses with the label 'root'.
scenes.narration: Each point where a branch splits is an internal node. It stands for an inferred ancestor of every lineage descending from it. The root, on the left, is the ancestor of everything on the tree.

scenes.tts: Lamprey is the outgroup, assumed to lie outside the rest. The root tells you which end is older. So for two nodes on one lineage, you can say which is more recent.
scenes.visual: Lamprey's branch is tinted and tagged 'outgroup'. The time arrow under the tree draws in from left ('older') to right ('today'); J and B drop small tick marks onto it, B's tick to the right of J's.
scenes.narration: Lamprey is the outgroup, assumed to lie outside the rest. The root tells you which end is older. So for two nodes on one lineage, you can say which is more recent.

scenes.tts: Now trace trout and shark back until their lines meet. They meet at node J. Then trace trout and human. They meet at node B.
scenes.visual: A GREY-BLUE line runs back from the trout tip and the shark tip and merges at J, which glows GREY-BLUE. Then a GOLD line runs back from trout and from human and merges at B, which glows GOLD.
scenes.narration: Now trace trout and shark back until their lines meet. They meet at node J. Then trace trout and human. They meet at node B.

scenes.tts: Node B descends from node J, so B is more recent. B is the most recent common ancestor of trout and human. That is the latest node from which both descend. Shark does not descend from B.
scenes.visual: B's tick on the time arrow sits to the right of J's, with the label 'more recent'. A label 'most recent common ancestor (MRCA)' attaches to the GOLD node B. The shark branch dims slightly to show it leaves the tree before B.
scenes.narration: Node B descends from node J, so B is more recent. B is the most recent common ancestor of trout and human. That is the latest node from which both descend. Shark does not descend from B.

scenes.tts: So a trout is more closely related to you than to a shark. It is equally close to the frog. A clade is an ancestor and all its descendants. Trout, frog and human form one clade.
scenes.visual: A GOLD rounded outline wraps B and the trout, frog and human tips, labelled 'clade'. The human and frog icons both get an '=' sign toward trout. The shark sits outside the outline.
scenes.narration: So a trout is more closely related to you than to a shark. It is equally close to the frog. A clade is an ancestor and all its descendants. Trout, frog and human form one clade.

scenes.tts: Now spin node T, like one arm of a mobile. Frog and human swap places on the page. Every clade keeps its members, so nothing about the history has changed.
scenes.visual: Node T rotates 180 degrees on its pivot; the frog and human tips swap vertical positions with a smooth swing. The GOLD clade outline stretches and follows them, never losing a member. Caption 'rotate a node = swap the two branches leaving it'.
scenes.narration: Now spin node T, like one arm of a mobile. Frog and human swap places on the page. Every clade keeps its members, so nothing about the history has changed.

scenes.tts: Now spin node B. Shark will no longer sit beside trout on the page. Does trout's closest relative change?
scenes.visual: A curved rotation arrow hovers over the GOLD node B, not yet moving. Question card: 'Spin node B. Does trout's closest relative change?'
scenes.narration: Now spin node B. Shark will no longer sit beside trout on the page. Does trout's closest relative change?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; a 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: No. The drawing changed, but the tree did not. Trout still meets frog and human at node B, and shark at node J. Tips side by side on the page are not, for that reason, closest relatives.
scenes.visual: Node B spins: trout swings to the bottom, the frog-human pair to the top, so shark now sits next to frog. The GOLD outline follows. The trace lines replay: trout to B (GOLD), trout to shark at J (GREY-BLUE). A stamp 'same tree' appears.
scenes.narration: No. The drawing changed, but the tree did not. Trout still meets frog and human at node B, and shark at node J. Tips side by side on the page are not, for that reason, closest relatives.

scenes.tts: One more misreading. Human sits at the end, so is it more evolved? No. Every living tip has had the same time since the root. Lampreys lack jaws, but they have derived features of their own.
scenes.visual: All five branches light at once from R to the 'today' end of the time arrow, each with an equal-length bracket 'same time since the root'. A small 'more evolved?' tag over the human tip is crossed out. The lamprey icon shows a schematic round mouth disc, labelled 'its own derived feature'.
scenes.narration: One more misreading. Human sits at the end, so is it more evolved? No. Every living tip has had the same time since the root. Lampreys lack jaws, but they have derived features of their own.

scenes.tts: So characters, not whole organisms, are ancestral or derived. And relatedness is read only at the nodes. Find the most recent common ancestor, and ignore how the drawing happens to look.
scenes.visual: The tree returns to its original drawing. The GOLD node B pulses; the tip order fades to grey, labelled 'drawing only'. Text appears: 'Read relatedness at the nodes.'
scenes.narration: So characters, not whole organisms, are ancestral or derived. And relatedness is read only at the nodes. Find the most recent common ancestor, and ignore how the drawing happens to look.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex, holding a small tree sign. Line: 'Relatedness lives in the most recent common ancestor.'
